newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish state-organised crime scandal widens.
newsitem.headline: Turkish state-organised crime scandal widens.

text.p: Turkey's police chief said on Friday his forces uncovered 25 crime gangs this year and threw out 150 police as a scandal over links between security forces and organised crime spread through the heart of the state.
"Since I took over this job (at the start of the year) some 25 gangs have been uncovered," police chief Alaattin Yuksel was quoted by the state-run Anatolian news agency as saying.

"In this period around 150 members of the security forces have been stripped of their duties. The papers are ready for the removal of 100 more of them," Yuksel said. He vowed to clean up the force no matter how many officers he had to sack.

A growing chorus of allegations around a car crash last week in which a top police official, a gangster wanted for murder and drug dealing and a former beauty queen were killed while travelling in the same car, has already brought down a minister.
Sedat Bucak, a Kurdish chieftain and government MP, was in the same car. He was secretly discharged from an Istanbul hospital early on Friday, hospital officials said.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and his deputy, Tansu Ciller, deny former police chief and interior minister Mehmet Agar's resignation last week had anything to do with the crash.
But Agar, from Ciller's True Path Party, said he resigned to clear the way for an investigation.
Some opposition MPs say the blame lies further up the political line.
A series of courts, a parliamentary commission and the Interior Ministry have begun to investigate the relationship among the personalities involved in the crash.
Prosecutors in the western town of Susurluk -- scene of the crash -- recommended investigation into a crime ring because guns, silencers and falsified documents were found in the car.
But political analysts and many MPs hold out little hope of a result. Leftist leader Deniz Baykal called on President Suleyman Demirel to intervene.
"Mr Demirel must call the leaders of all parties in parliament together and everyone must reveal what they know," Baykal told a meeting in the western town of Izmir.
The crash reignited a scandal over links between the state and organised crime that came to light earlier this year with the arrest of security officials for forming a criminal gang.
The Turkish public got a snippet of the murky, complicated "gangland-state" activities when the leaders of the group, the Soylemez brothers, turned out to be feuding with the Bucak clan.

Police have revealed since that the Soylemez gang had been planning a helicopter attack -- with equipment obtained from security forces -- against some of the Bucak family, many of whom are armed by the state to help in the fight against separatist rebel Kurds in the southeast.
Opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz said the recent findings showed that no one was safe in the country.
"The state, the security forces of the state, are supposed to protect our lives," Yilmaz told a news programme on the private Kanal D television channel late on Thursday.
"If even part of the state's security forces are involved in such things, who is left to protect us? Are you not afraid?" he asked Ugur Dundar, presenter of the Arena news programme.
Yilmaz, a former prime minister, suggested many unsolved crimes, including the high-profile killing of a casino chain-owner in July, were state-sponsored killings.

Yuksel denied police had knowingly given Abdullah Catli, the gangster who died in the car crash, a "green passport" -- given to state officials going abroad. Catli, on the run for nearly 20 years, obtained the passport with the use of forged signatures and false identification, he said.
